articles.title: Varanasi passenger boards overnight train with confirmed berth A1/54, finds no such seat in coach with 52 berths; Railways say software glitch led to wrong allotment
articles.summary: VARANASI: A passenger travelling on a confirmed ticket aboard a North Eastern Railway (NER) train found that his allotted berth did not exist in the
articles.body: VARANASI: A passenger travelling on a confirmed ticket aboard a North Eastern Railway (NER) train found that his allotted berth did not exist in the coach, prompting the Railways to acknowledge a software glitch that led to the discrepancy.Ishan Bajpai was travelling on Train No. 15132 from Varanasi City to Gorakhpur Junction on November 22 when he discovered that his confirmed berth, A1/54, was missing. The AC 2-tier coach had only 52 berths, leaving him without an allotted seat despite holding a confirmed ticket.Bajpai flagged the issue on X around 10.45pm, expressing frustration over being left without a berth during an overnight journey. He also said he had registered a complaint through railway helpline 139.Responding to his post, the Railways' official grievance redressal handle said the matter had been escalated to the concerned official. It also sought his mobile number through a direct message to facilitate immediate action and advised him to use the RailMadad portal or helpline 139.A North Eastern Railway spokesperson from the Varanasi division said the department immediately responded to the passenger's post on X, regretting the inconvenience caused to him and another passenger."Both were accommodated on other berths in the same train. articles.title: Black Friday em Campina Grande: 5 lojas são autuadas pelo MP-Procon | G1
articles.standfirst: Programa de Proteção e Defesa do Consumidor (MP-Procon) realizou operação nesta sexta-feira (27), dia da Black Friday. Medidas foram tomadas contra os estabelecimentos.
articles.summary: A operação do MP-Procon na Black Friday em Campina Grande flagrou a falta de preços históricos e de informações sobre o estoque em cinco estabelecimentos da cidade.
articles.body:
Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

O Programa de Proteção e Defesa do Consumidor (MP-Procon), do Ministério Público da Paraíba (MPPB), autuou cinco estabelecimentos comerciais por irregularidades durante a Black Friday, em Campina Grande , nesta sexta-feira (27).

Entre os problemas encontrados nos cinco estabelecimentos autuados estão:

Ausência de informações claras e visíveis sobre os produtos participantes das promoções;

Falta de divulgação da quantidade de itens disponíveis em estoque;

Inexistência de listas acessíveis aos consumidores com a identificação dos produtos em oferta.

Em uma das lojas fiscalizadas, também foi constatada ainda a ausência de informações sobre os preços praticados nos últimos três meses para os produtos anunciados na Black Friday. A equipe de fiscalização verificou ainda a falta de exemplar do Código de Defesa do Consumidor (CDC) disponível para consulta dos clientes.

Operação autua cinco estabelecimentos por irregularidades durante a Black Friday, em Campina Grande — Foto: Brenda Lima/PMBV/Divulgação

Outro problema apontado pela fiscalização foi a disponibilização de informações sobre as ofertas anunciadas nos canais digitais das empresas, especialmente a existência de listas físicas, em local visível e acessível nas lojas, com a identificação dos produtos participantes das promoções e as respectivas quantidades disponíveis.

De acordo com o Ministério Público, oito estabelecimentos comerciais foram fiscalizados ao todo. Três deles estavam em conformidade com o exigido pela legislação.

articles.title: Shoppers helped pay Trump’s tariffs. Now Target, Best Buy, and Kohl’s are booking $387 million in refunds
articles.summary: The three retailers booked $387 million in refund benefits last quarter, while Walmart and Target say they're cutting prices rather than paying shoppers back...
articles.body:
American consumers helped foot the bill for President Donald Trump's tariffs as retailers passed higher import costs on through price increases. Now the refunds are flowing back, and they are showing up in retailers' profits rather than in shoppers' bank accounts.

Best Buy and Kohl's both reported better-than-expected quarterly results on Tuesday, after Target beat expectations last week. Together, the three retailers recognized $387 million in tariff refund benefits in their latest quarters.

The money traces back to February, when the Supreme Court ruled that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) did not authorize the president to impose tariffs, invalidating a significant portion of Trump's tariff regime. As of Nov. 5, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) had certified approximately $128.4 billion in tariff refunds, including interest, and sent them to the Treasury Department for payment, according to a Nov. 10 filing with the U.S. Court of International Trade.

Tariff refunds are boosting retailers' profits

Kohl's reported third-quarter comparable sales growth of just 1.2%, yet its net income jumped to $254 million from $8 million a year earlier. Much of that came from one-time items: a $137 million tax benefit, a $61 million gain from the sale of two properties, and $45 million in tariff refund benefits, according to the company's third-quarter earnings release .

The department store chain has received approximately $190 million in tariff refunds this fiscal year. It now expects those refunds to add $1.03 to its full-year earnings per share, nearly a quarter of its raised forecast of $4.30 to $4.50.

Best Buy reported comparable sales growth of 6.1%, its strongest in five years, in Jason Bonfig's first earnings report as CEO . Net income more than doubled to $353 million from $140 million, according to the company's earnings release .

In May 2025, Best Buy's then-CEO Corie Barry said the electronics retailer had already raised prices on some products to offset the costs of Trump's tariffs. This quarter, the company recorded $41 million in tariff refund benefits, which helped lift profitability.

Target has recognized approximately $1.3 billion in tariff refund benefits in the first nine months of its fiscal year, including $301 million in the third quarter alone. Its quarterly net income rose to $1.2 billion from $689 million, and tariff refunds accounted for $228 million of that after taxes, or nearly a fifth, according to Target's third-quarter results .

articles.title: Google Gemini may expose private emails to reviewers
articles.summary: A researcher claims Google Gemini pulled private Gmail billing details into chats, and Google confirms some connected-app data may face human review.
articles.body: Think about everything sitting in your Gmail inbox right now. Maybe there's a conversation with your doctor, a recent bank statement or a personal message you never intended anyone else to read. Your Google Drive may hold years of private documents. You probably don't spend much time thinking about who might see that information beyond the people you share it with. But what happens when you connect those services to Google's Gemini AI assistant? An independent researcher has raised concerns about how Gemini handles information retrieved from connected Gmail and Google Drive accounts. The findings prompted questions about whether some private content could end up in conversations reviewed by humans. We contacted Google, and the company confirmed that some information retrieved from connected Gmail and Drive accounts may be seen by human reviewers under certain circumstances. Google stressed that these connections are off by default. Here's what you should know before giving Gemini access to your personal information. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. AI CHATBOT PRIVACY: WHAT YOUR AI MAY KNOW ABOUT YOU Researcher raises concerns about Google Gemini privacy An independent researcher using the name thisisme6598 published findings on GitHub, raising questions about the way Gemini retrieves information from connected Gmail and Google Drive accounts. The researcher tested Gemini using a personal Google Account with connected apps enabled. According to the published findings, Gemini sometimes retrieved information from emails or files during conversations without someone explicitly asking it to search Gmail or Drive. For example, the researcher described asking Gemini whether an internet service bill seemed too expensive. During some tests, Gemini reportedly retrieved billing information from Gmail, including payment amounts, account details and confirmation numbers. In certain instances, the researcher reported that Gemini returned several sentences directly from an email and, in some tests, the entire email, including its headers. The researcher argues that this behavior creates a privacy concern because information retrieved into a Gemini conversation may become eligible for human review. However, the published findings do not establish that a human reviewer actually accessed the researcher's emails. Google told CyberGuy that the reported retrieval was standard behavior for someone who had voluntarily connected their apps. The company also emphasized that retrieved files remain visible only to the authenticated account holder and are not exposed publicly through this process. Can human reviewers see your Gmail and Drive information through Gemini? Yes, under certain circumstances. Google's own Connected Apps privacy documentation confirms that trained human reviewers, including service providers, may review a subset of information processed through Gemini's connected apps. That information can include summaries or excerpts from relevant Gmail messages and Google Drive documents. In some cases, Google acknowledges that reviewers may see a complete email or file if it is short or especially relevant to the request. Google also says human reviewers may access some Gmail inbox content when investigating abuse or harm or responding to submitted feedback. The company uses these reviews to evaluate Gemini's responses and improve its services. Simply using Gmail or Google Drive does not subject your private content to this review process. The concern involves information retrieved after someone voluntarily connects those services to consumer Gemini. Google says it does not train generative AI models directly on someone's entire Gmail inbox or Drive. However, relevant information processed during Gemini conversations may be used for model improvement, depending on account settings. Google specifically warns against connecting apps containing confidential information someone would be uncomfortable having a reviewer see. What Google told CyberGuy about Gemini privacy We contacted Google directly to ask whether human reviewers could access Gmail messages or Drive files processed through the consumer Gemini app. We also asked whether the company had changed its privacy disclosures, notified existing customers and provided ways to prevent human review. A Google spokesperson told CyberGuy: "Gmail and Google Drive’s core privacy protections remain unchanged, and your private emails and files are not reviewed by humans simply by using Gmail, Drive, or built-in Workspace features. Connecting those apps to the consumer Gemini app is off by default — it’s an optional way to get more personalized, time-saving answers across your Google apps when you want them. Users can disconnect their apps in Gemini settings at any time without losing access to Gemini’s core features." Google also confirmed that when someone connects their apps to consumer Gemini with activity saving enabled, a small subset of conversations may undergo human review. Those conversations can contain relevant information retrieved from connected services. Before trained service providers review the material, Google says it separates the conversations from the associated Google Account and takes steps to reduce identifying information. The company also disputes the suggestion that the researcher's findings demonstrate public exposure of private files. Did Google change its Gemini privacy promises? Another part of the controversy involves changes to Google's public privacy disclosures. In Oct. 2023, Google published a blog post about its approach to generative AI privacy. The company said that content from Gmail, Docs and Drive accessed through Bard's Workspace extensions would not be seen by human reviewers or used to train the Bard model. On Oct. 16, 2026, Google added an update to that same blog post. The new language explains that Google has introduced additional optional features allowing people to connect Workspace information to other Google services. Google says that when someone enables these newer features, a subset of the information may be used to train generative AI models, depending on their settings. It may also undergo human review in limited circumstances. The researcher argues that the change represents a reversal of Google's earlier privacy commitment. However, Google's original statement concerned Bard's Workspace extensions, while the updated disclosure addresses newer connected features. The available evidence does not establish that Google quietly changed the underlying handling of information in existing connections. We asked Google whether people who previously connected their accounts were notified about the updated disclosures or asked to provide additional consent. Google's response did not directly address those questions. Instead, the company emphasized that the newer connections are optional and can be disabled. That leaves an important question about how clearly Google communicates changes to its AI privacy practices, particularly as new features gain access to more personal information. APPLE TIGHTENS MAC SECURITY AS AI AGENTS SEEK YOUR FILES What happens to your information after human review? Google says it disconnects conversations from the associated Google Account before sending them to trained service providers for routine review. The company also takes steps to reduce personal information. However, removing account identifiers does not necessarily eliminate every sensitive detail contained in an email excerpt or document summary. Google's Gemini Apps Privacy Hub explains that conversations reviewed by service providers may be retained for up to three years, even after someone deletes the corresponding activity from their Google Account. Turning off Gemini's History setting, previously called Keep Activity, prevents future conversations from being used to train generative AI models unless someone submits feedback. However, Google may still process conversations for security and safety purposes, including with help from human reviewers. On Nov. 16, 2026, Google announced changes to its Gemini privacy controls. Under the previous policy, Google retained conversations for up to 72 hours when Keep Activity was turned off. Under the new policy, Google will retain conversations for approximately two months when History is turned off. The company is rolling out these changes globally over several weeks. How to protect your Gmail and Google Drive privacy If you use Gemini, it's worth checking which accounts and services you've connected. You may find that you don't need every feature enabled. Here are some settings worth reviewing. Disconnect Gmail and Drive from Gemini Google groups Gmail and Drive under Google Workspace in its connected-app settings. Here's how to check the connection on a computer. If you see a different menu, look for Connected Apps in Gemini's settings. Google offers different connection controls depending on account eligibility and available features. You can reconnect supported services later if you decide to use them. Turn off Gemini History (formerly Keep Activity) If you want to prevent future conversations from being used to train Google's generative AI models, review this setting. Turning off History stops future chats from being used to train generative AI models unless you choose to submit feedback. Some connected apps, including Google Workspace, become unavailable. Google may still process conversations for security and safety purposes. Depending on whether the latest privacy update has reached your account, conversations may be retained for up to 72 hours under the previous policy or approximately two months under the new policy. WHAT YOUR INTERNET PROVIDER, WEBSITES AND ADVERTISERS SEE Turn off AI training without deleting your Gemini history Google is introducing a separate privacy control that lets you keep your Gemini conversation history while opting out of generative AI model training. If the new setting is available on your account, here's how to find it on a computer. Google says future chats will no longer be used to train generative AI models unless you submit feedback. However, human review may still occur for other service improvements and safety purposes. If you want to prevent Gemini from retrieving information from Gmail and Drive, disconnect Google Workspace separately. Delete previous Gemini conversations Disconnecting an app does not automatically delete information from earlier Gemini conversations. Google says Gemini may still use information from previously saved chats even after you disconnect the original app. That's why it's important to both disconnect the app and delete conversations containing sensitive information. Remember that previously reviewed information may remain subject to Google's separate retention policies, even after you delete your activity. Avoid sharing sensitive information with AI assistants Think carefully before giving an AI assistant access to confidential documents or personal communications. If you don't need Gemini to retrieve information from Gmail or Drive, leave those connections disabled. Also, remember that uploading a document directly into Gemini creates a separate privacy consideration. Google says uploaded content may be used to improve its services when History, previously called Keep Activity, is enabled, potentially with help from human reviewers. Whether that content is used to train generative AI models also depends on your training settings and whether you submit feedback. Does this Gemini privacy concern affect business accounts? Google says the connected-app disclosures involved in this controversy apply to personal Google Accounts using consumer Gemini. Business, Enterprise and Education accounts covered by Google Workspace commercial terms have different privacy protections. According to Google's response to CyberGuy, customer data governed by those commercial terms is not reviewed by humans or used to train foundational AI models. If you use Gemini through an employer or school, your organization's settings and agreements determine which features are available and how information is handled. The important point is that the consumer Gemini privacy rules discussed here should not automatically be applied to commercial Workspace accounts. Kurt's key takeaways I can understand why someone would want Gemini to search their Gmail or find a document buried in Google Drive. We've all wasted time digging through old emails looking for something we need. Having an AI assistant do that work sounds pretty appealing. But I think Google has a responsibility to make the privacy implications much clearer before someone connects an account. Most people probably don't expect information pulled from their private emails to become part of a conversation that could eventually be reviewed by another human being. I appreciate that Google responded to our questions and explained the safeguards it uses. Still, I would have liked a more direct answer about whether existing customers were notified when the privacy disclosures changed. If you're giving an AI assistant access to years of personal information, you deserve to know exactly how that information might be handled. Personally, I'd leave Gmail and Drive disconnected unless I had a specific reason to use those features. Would you trust an AI assistant with access to years of your private emails if you knew some of that information could be seen by human reviewers? Or has Google crossed a privacy line, even with your permission? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com. articles.title: Hackers break into US Air Force cloud computing platform: Report
articles.summary: Hackers breached the Air Force’s main cloud computing platform in recent weeks, risking sensitive data, according to a new report from Reuters, the latest in a string of cyber incidents and outages at government agencies. Reuters reported Friday that according to three sources, hackers broke into the Air Force’s Cloud One platform, which hosts sensitive…
articles.body:
Hackers breached the Air Force’s main cloud computing platform in recent weeks, risking sensitive data, according to a new report from Reuters, the latest in a string of cyber incidents and outages at government agencies.

Reuters reported Friday that according to three sources, hackers broke into the Air Force’s Cloud One platform, which hosts sensitive tactical, personnel and logistics data.

Two of the sources told Reuters the hack had been found in the past month or so, as the system was being upgraded. Reuters reported that it had not uncovered who the hackers are, how far they had gotten into the system and if data was swiped from Cloud One.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

The reported hack follows other breaches in recent days.

The CIA said Tuesday that some of its unclassified systems were exposed in a hack. The Office of the Director of National Intelligence said its systems were also impacted by the breach.

The Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network said Thursday it’s investigating an intrusion into some online systems.

Federal agencies have also been hit by outages that spurred widespread fears of malicious activity.

Last week , the National Security Agency faced a network outage, disrupting a classified internal network.

The Federal Aviation Administration issued a rare nationwide ground stop earlier this month, lasting for over four hours. Authorities pointed to a router in Arkansas and a Texas-based radar site as the two probable reasons behind the outage.

On Sunday, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said that Americans should get ready for upgrades to aging infrastructure and multiple systems. He advised that there would be “bumps in the road” in the wake of the recent tech failures.

“The American people should be prepared for a great deal of investment in upgrading our systems,” he told CNN’s Dana Bash. “They should be prepared for investment in cybersecurity, and they should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road.”

When reached for comment, a Pentagon official told The Hill that, “As a matter of policy and operations security, the Department of War does not comment on the status of our networks.”

“We refer you to the U.S. Air Force for more information,” the official added.

articles.title: Military says it disabled vessel that ‘attempted to run the U.S. naval blockade’ against Iran
articles.summary: American forces on Thursday disabled a commercial vessel attempting to bypass the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports, U.S. Central Command (Centcom) said Friday. The crew of the bulk carrier “attempted to run the U.S. naval blockade, despite multiple warnings” after departing the southern port city of Bandar Abbas, Iran, Centcom said in a release.…
articles.body:
American forces on Thursday disabled a commercial vessel attempting to bypass the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports, U.S. Central Command (Centcom) said Friday.

The crew of the bulk carrier “attempted to run the U.S. naval blockade, despite multiple warnings” after departing the southern port city of Bandar Abbas, Iran, Centcom said in a release .

“A U.S. military aircraft launched precision munitions that struck the stern of Palau-flagged M/V Pacific Archer,” the command added. “The ship’s propulsion was ultimately disabled and the civilian crew was unharmed.”

Centcom also shared an unclassified, eight-second video of a munition striking the vessel.

American forces resumed blockading Iranian ports in the middle of July, after previously doing so from mid-April until late June amid the U.S. and Israeli war on Iran.

Adm. Brad Cooper, the commander of Centcom, said on Oct. 16 that the blockade had cost the Islamic Republic $25 billion in oil revenue — directly impacting Iran’s Revolutionary Guard.

“As a point of emphasis, with the exception of the humanitarian assistance we’ve allowed in, Iran has no exports and no imports by sea,” Cooper said in a video . “The sum total of these actions has imposed devastating costs on Iran’s security apparatus and the IRGC specifically.”

Centcom marked 130 consecutive days of the blockade last weekend, writing on the social platform X it is “preventing” the Revolutionary Guard “from exporting billions of dollars in crude oil.”

The command said Friday its forces have “redirected” 158 compliant commercial vessels and “disabled” six others that refused to comply with the blockade.

“All mariners operating in the Gulf of Oman and approaches to the Strait of Hormuz are urged to heed blockade warnings issued by CENTCOM forces,” it added.

The Iran war will hit the nine-month mark on Saturday. President Trump said Thursday the conflict will end “sort of whenever” he decides to wind it down.

During a Senate Armed Services Committee hearing on Nov. 13, Pentagon budget official Arthur Miller told Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) that the conflict had cost taxpayers $48.3 billion .

The figure included munitions costs, equipment replacement costs and operational costs, but did not account for total damage to U.S. military facilities in the Middle East by Iranian forces, Miller noted.

articles.title: Hackers breach Air Force's flagship cloud computing platform, report says
articles.summary: Hackers reportedly breached the U.S. Air Force's Cloud One platform, putting sensitive personnel and logistics data at risk, sources told Reuters.
articles.body: Hackers reportedly breached the U.S. Air Force's flagship Cloud One computing platform, potentially accessing a wide swath of logistic and personnel data, three sources reportedly told Reuters. The hack, which was discovered within the past month during system updating, may have jeopardized "a vast swathe of sensitive tactical, personnel and logistics data," according to Reuters. "The Department of the Air Force does not comment on the security posture, vulnerabilities, or operational status of specific networks and systems. We continuously take prudent measures to protect Department information, systems, and mission capabilities. Ensuring the security, resilience, and availability of our most critical warfighting assets remains a top priority," an Air Force spokesperson told Fox News Digital in a statement. PENTAGON DATA BREACH EXPOSES SOCIAL SECURITY NUMBERS, PERSONAL INFO OF 2.76M US MILITARY, CIVILIAN PERSONNEL "The Department continues to assess and modernize its enterprise cloud capabilities to meet evolving mission, security, resilience, and user requirements. Decisions regarding technical architecture, workload placement, contracts, and future capabilities are made through established governance, acquisition, and risk-management processes," the statement concluded. Reuters' sources were not able to identify the identity of the hackers, the extent of their intrusion or the scope of what data they may have been able to collect, if any. The discovery of the breach has led to disruption across the Cloud One platform, the sources told the outlet. Cloud One is a proprietary system the Air Force launched in 2017 to combine the capabilities of the four major information technology platforms the department uses: Microsoft, Amazon, Oracle and Google-owner Alphabet. PENTAGON DATA BREACH EXPOSES RECORDS OF OVER 3M PEOPLE The Air Force's Cloud-Based Command and Control, a system that coordinates air defense radars, and the Theater Integrated Combat Munitions System, which tracks bombs and missiles across more than 200 global Air Force locations, are part of the Cloud One platform. "A breach here is a big deal," one source told Reuters. CIA HIT BY CYBER BREACH THAT EXPOSED UNCLASSIFIED DATA ON INTELLIGENCE ANALYSIS NETWORK: SOURCES The reported breach is the latest in a series of recently disclosed hacks on government and military systems. The FBI's National Crime Information Center has been the victim of hacking twice in the past few months, CNN reported last Friday. The CIA also recently suffered a data breach that exposed unclassified data used by law enforcement across the country, sources told Fox News. HOMELAND SECURITY DATA LEAK EXPOSES 41K WORKERS A late October hack on Department of Homeland Security (DHS) systems exposed the personal information of over 41,000 DHS employees, including undercover Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers. A recent cyberattack on the Department of Treasury disabled portions of the department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN). TECH OUTAGE CASCADE EXPOSES US VULNERABILITIES TO FOREIGN CYBER THREATS Additionally, the National Security Agency (NSA) made headlines when sources reportedly told CNN the agency's internal communication network was suffering from a service outage. In 2023, Cloud One leadership, in an article on FedScoop.com, touted Cloud One's 100% success rate in combatting adversarial intrusions. "There is no room for error when it comes to security," Cloud One's leadership wrote. We refer you to the U.S. Air Force for more information."

articles.title: Meta whistleblower says gag order reminiscent of ‘1984’
articles.summary: Sarah Wynn-Williams, a former Facebook employee whose book warned about the company’s power, said a gag order preventing her from speaking about the tech giant was akin to the reality in George Orwell’s “1984” novel. “Control what people are allowed to remember or what they are allowed to know, and you control what they are…
articles.body:
Sarah Wynn-Williams, a former Facebook employee whose book warned about the company’s power, said a gag order preventing her from speaking about the tech giant was akin to the reality in George Orwell’s “1984” novel.

“Control what people are allowed to remember or what they are allowed to know, and you control what they are able to imagine,” she wrote in a Guardian opinion piece published Friday. “Control what they can imagine, and you have already chosen their future for them.”

Facebook’s parent company Meta and other corporations, she wrote, have “mastered corporate lawfare” and can let “slip the dogs of law on individuals who don’t have millions of pounds to defend themselves against” what she called “attacks” by those companies.

Wynn-Williams worked at Facebook from 2011-17, rising to the social media company’s global public policy director. The company fired her in 2017, a move Wynn-Williams has argued was retaliation for reporting her boss, Joel Kaplan, for sexual harassment.

Wynn-Williams released a book about experience at Facebook in 2025. But Meta, led by CEO Mark Zuckerberg, secured an emergency ruling by the American Arbitration Association in March of that year, which barred Wynn-Williams from publicly promoting her memoir, titled, “Careless People: A Cautionary Tale of Power, Greed and Lost Idealism.”

During testimony before Senate lawmakers in April 2025, Wynn-Williams said Meta executives “lied about what they were doing with the Chinese Communist Party to employees, shareholders, Congress and the American public.” Meta has pushed back on those claims.

Wynn-Williams wrote in the Guardian that it is “hard to explain” living under a gag order, again comparing it to an Orwellian situation.

“Orwell gave us the thoughtcrime: you don’t have to act against the Party to be guilty,” she wrote. “You just have to think the wrong thing. That’s what it feels like. To worry you might think the wrong thing and it could slip out.”

The former Facebook employee sued Meta in June, with her lawyers arguing the company is “punishing” her for “disclosing its illegal and indefensible workplace conditions” and corporate misconduct.

“Meta has engaged in surveillance to monitor Ms. Wynn-Williams’s speech and associations,” lawyers for Wynn-Williams wrote in a 57-page filing in U.S. District Court in Northern California.

“It has used the results of that surveillance to seek sanctions against Ms. Wynn-Williams for a wide range of public appearances and, in recent months, for nearly every public appearance she has made, even though she has never spoken about her book or about Meta at any appearance,” her attorneys added.

In her Guardian piece, Wynn-Williams wrote “it has felt as if certain sectors of society, including technology companies, act with impunity.”

She added, “I worry about all the powerful people who continue to benefit from silence and deprive us, the public, of information that can lead to warnings and ideally accountability. I worry we will only be allowed the truth about these companies when it no longer matters.”

images.caption: Sarah Wynn-Williams, Facebook’s former director of Global Public Policy, testifies before the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism on Capitol Hill, Wednesday, April 9, 2025, in Washington. (AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein)
